target.item_text:
The Unicorn Anthology
Paperback – April 19, 2019

“What a treasure trove!”―Sarah Beth Durst, author of Queen of the Blood Unicorns: Not just for virgins anymore. Here are sixteen lovely, powerful, intricate, and unexpected unicorn tales from fantasy icons including Garth Nix, Peter S. Beagle, Patricia A. McKillip, Bruce Coville, Carrie Vaughn, and more. In this volume you will find two would-be hunters who enlist an innkeeper to find a priest hiding the secret of the last unicorn. A time traveler tries to corral an unruly mythological beast that might never have existed at all. The lover and ex-boyfriend of a dying woman join forces to find a miraculous remedy in New York City. And a small-town writer of historical romances discovers a sliver of a mysterious horn in a slice of apple pie.
target.review:
I guess if you were to ask people who'd be the best choice to be editor of an anthology of Unicorn related short stories, few would begrudge Peter S. Beagle that position.

Varied in tone and genre (varying sub-genres of fantasy, horror, noir, etc), like any good short story collection should be, I found this anthology very satisfying. You get all manner of stories involving unicorns, some a bit more magical than others, but all pretty interesting.

You get some big names here, both old masters of their craft and younger authors. Might be a little too much unicorn for some people, so maybe you can read it in parallel to another book in order if you're not so much into the mythic horned horses (who except young girls is?), but all in all it's a pretty good anthology.

demonstrations.item_text:

demonstrations.review: Pretty interesting premise explained in a way that is accessible to anyone regardless of academic background. Explains the cultural generation gap pretty well and is a great starting point to her other book that delves more deeply into it, the Narcissism Epidemic.

demonstrations.item_text:
The Shepherd's Crown (Tiffany Aching, 5)
Hardcover – September 1, 2015

Fantasy grandmaster Sir Terry Pratchett's final Discworld novel, and the fifth to feature the witch Tiffany Aching. A SHIVERING OF WORLDS Deep in the Chalk, something is stirring. The owls and the foxes can sense it, and Tiffany Aching feels it in her boots. An old enemy is gathering strength. This is a time of endings and beginnings, old friends and new, a blurring of edges and a shifting of power. Now Tiffany stands between the light and the dark, the good and the bad. As the fairy horde prepares for invasion, Tiffany must summon all the witches to stand with her. To protect the land. Her land. There will be a reckoning. . . . THE FINAL DISCWORLD NOVEL The five funny and fabulous Tiffany Aching adventures are: The Wee Free Men The Wee Free Men A Hat Full of Sky A Hat Full of Sky Wintersmith Wintersmith I Shall Wear Midnight I Shall Wear Midnight The Shepherd’s Crown The Shepherd’s Crown Tiffany’s mentors, Granny Weatherwax and Nanny Ogg, star in the novels Equal Rites , Wyrd Sisters , Witches Abroad , Lords and Ladies , Maskerade , and Carpe Jugulum . And don’t miss Terry Pratchett’s hilarious and wise Discworld novel The Amazing Maurice and His Educated Rodents !
demonstrations.review:
"The Shepherd's Crown" is a return to form by the author, whose later novels set in the Discworld seemed a bit off somehow. Considering that he wrote them while suffering from a form of Alzheimer's, and that his worst books are pretty much better than most stuff out there anyway, this is no small feat.

Taking us back to Tiffany Aching and the Chalk, as well as Lancre and other familiar places and faces, the novel is a bittersweet farewell to a series spanning more than thirty years in real time and more than forty books.

When I have children I will read all of Terry Pratchett's novels to them. And I do mean ALL sixty-odd of them. Everything you need to know about life and people is there somewhere, provided you take a look.

demonstrations.item_text:
Paddle Your Own Canoe: One Man's Fundamentals for Delicious Living
Hardcover – Illustrated, October 1, 2013

Parks and Recreation actor and Making It co-host Nick Offerman shares his humorous fulminations on life, manliness, meat, and much more in this New York Times bestseller. Growing a perfect moustache, grilling red meat, wooing a woman—who better to deliver this tutelage than the always charming, always manly Nick Offerman, best known as Parks and Recreation ’s Ron Swanson?  Combining his trademark comic voice and very real expertise in woodworking—he runs his own woodshop— Paddle Your Own Canoe features tales from Offerman’s childhood in small-town Minooka, Illinois—“I grew up literally in the middle of a cornfield”—to his theater days in Chicago, beginnings as a carpenter/actor and the hilarious and magnificent seduction of his now-wife Megan Mullally.   It also offers hard-bitten battle strategies in the arenas of manliness, love, style, religion, woodworking, and outdoor recreation, among many other savory entrees.A mix of amusing anecdotes, opinionated lessons and rants, sprinkled with offbeat gaiety, Paddle Your Own Canoe will not only tickle readers pink but may also rouse them to put down their smart phones, study a few sycamore leaves, and maybe even hand craft (and paddle) their own canoes.
demonstrations.review:
Nick Offerman is a great comedic actor as well as a very funny guy when not acting. This book shares his views on how to live your life properly by narrating the lessons he's learned since childhood from his family, mentors, and friends.

One thing I really enjoyed was how he makes fun of his public persona, so ingrained as Ron Swanson from "Parks and Recreation," but then takes the opportunity to point out how he isn't Ron Swanson, and even how Ron Swanson's philosophies can be misunderstood. His narrative voice is so distinctive, that you can't help but hear his voice in your head when readings this book.

I think it's cool that his lessons boil basically down to "Try to be capable, help each other, and do your own thing without imposing your way of life on others." Most things wrong in the world seem to stem from people who don't stick to those simple rules.

demonstrations.review: Just as good as the rest. As long as Doescher keeps writing them I'll keep buying them and enjoying the hell out of them. target.item_text:
American Nations: A History of the Eleven Rival Regional Cultures of North America
Paperback – September 25, 2012

* A New Republic Best Book of the Year * The Globalist Top Books of the Year * Winner of the Maine Literary Award for Non-fiction * Particularly relevant in understanding who voted for who in this presidential election year, this is an endlessly fascinating look at American regionalism and the eleven "nations" that continue to shape North America According to award-winning journalist and historian Colin Woodard, North America is made up of eleven distinct nations, each with its own unique historical roots. In American Nations he takes readers on a journey through the history of our fractured continent, offering a revolutionary and revelatory take on American identity, and how the conflicts between them have shaped our past and continue to mold our future. From the Deep South to the Far West, to Yankeedom to El Norte, Woodard (author of American Character: A History of the Epic Struggle Between Individual Liberty and the Common Good ) reveals how each region continues to uphold its distinguishing ideals and identities today, with results that can be seen in the composition of the U.S. Congress or on the county-by-county election maps of any hotly contested election in our history. This updated edition brings the story to the post-pandemic era.
target.review: This book covers the history of the US starting at 1590 thru 2010.  It focuses upon the characteristics of the populations who migrated to 11 various regions.  It contains so much information that I did not know about. He paints a picture of the Puritans as pretty horrific people - - at least if you think disfiguring Quakers by slitting their nostrils or branding their faces with an H for heretic is horrible. The Puritans did this for easy identification. He says (p. 57), "According to a central myth of American history, the founders  ... were champions of religious freedom. ... [this] is entirely false." They believed in their own religious freedom, but if you don't agree with them on how to live you had better not try to live amongst them. "Puritans doled out death sentences for infractions such as adultery, blasphemy ... and even teenage rebellion." This book has been an eye opener. I know that no group or nation is perfect or even close to perfect, but the self-seeking and inhumanity was beyond what I had thought.  Woodard’s presentation reveals what today are nuances of our history including motivations of various groups and states.

For example, there are no books in the house because the family is too poor to be able to buy any books. Reading to him or herself necessitates the child having a relatively large vocabulary so 8 years old might be a minimum. One such example I came upon is the word "sob." A 6 year old is unlikely to know this word. Anyway, get ready for an absolutely warm and wonderful read with your child or grandchild. I read this (and the many other books in the series) to my three children and so far to one grandchild.

demonstrations.item_text:
The Social Animal: The Hidden Sources of Love, Character, and Achievement
Hardcover – March 8, 2011

With unequaled insight and brio, David Brooks, the New York Times columnist and bestselling author of Bobos in Paradise, has long explored and explained the way we live. Now, with the intellectual curiosity and emotional wisdom that make his columns among the most read in the nation, Brooks turns to the building blocks of human flourishing in a multilayered, profoundly illuminating work grounded in everyday life.This is the story of how success happens. It is told through the lives of one composite American couple, Harold and Erica—how they grow, push forward, are pulled back, fail, and succeed. Distilling a vast array of information into these two vividly realized characters, Brooks illustrates a fundamental new understanding of human nature. A scientific revolution has occurred—we have learned more about the human brain in the last thirty years than we had in the previous three thousand. The unconscious mind, it turns out, is most of the mind—not a dark, vestigial place but a creative and enchanted one, where most of the brain’s work gets done. This is the realm of emotions, intuitions, biases, longings, genetic predispositions, personality traits, and social norms: the realm where character is formed and where our most important life decisions are made. The natural habitat of The Social Animal. Drawing on a wealth of current research from numerous disciplines, Brooks takes Harold and Erica from infancy to school; from the “odyssey years” that have come to define young adulthood to the high walls of poverty; from the nature of attachment, love, and commitment, to the nature of effective leadership. He reveals the deeply social aspect of our very minds and exposes the bias in modern culture that overemphasizes rationalism, individualism, and IQ. Along the way, he demolishes conventional definitions of success while looking toward a culture based on trust and humility. The Social Animal is a moving and nuanced intellectual adventure, a story of achievement and a defense of progress. Impossible to put down, it is an essential book for our time, one that will have broad social impact and will change the way we see ourselves and the world.
demonstrations.review:
David Brooks' The Social Animal is a very well written tour of the last 50 years of social science research. He presents this material in an interesting almost novel like manner by tracing the lives of two fictious people. The end notes provide a useful tool for further reading. If your spouse, sibling, or running partner has an interest in this sort of material, you can have a most interesting discussion/interaction by reading this book, one chapter at a time, and discussing the chapter you have just read. There is so much material to think about that you should not read several chapters and then discuss these all at once.

Much of the research reveals "facts" that appear to be obvious, but many of the "facts" are surprising. In only one instance, concerning whether or not more homework leads to better school performance, I found that the backup research lacked validity. This book is a great vehicle for learning about the progress made in social science over the last 50 years. I recommend this book without reservation.

Blood on the Tracks (Sydney Rose Parnell Book 1)
Kindle Edition

An Amazon Charts bestseller. A young woman is found brutally murdered, and the main suspect is the victim’s fiancé, a hideously scarred Iraq War vet known as the Burned Man. Hide (Detective Harriet Foster Book 1)

From acclaimed author Tracy Clark comes a page-turning mystery featuring hard-boiled Chicago detective Harriet Foster, who’s on the hunt for a serial killer with a deadly affinity for redheads. Detective Harriet Foster is on the case, even though she’s still grieving the sudden death of her partner. As a Black woman in a male-dominated department, Foster anticipates a rocky road ahead acclimating to a new team—and building trust with her new partner isn’t coming easily. demonstrations.review: All three books were intense, had to be read from start to finish with no break.  TR Ragan' s other books are just as enthralling.  I recommend all of them.  Couldn't put any of them down without finishing them in one sitting.

The Dying Hour introduces Jason Wade, a rookie crime reporter with The Seattle Mirror, a loner who grew up in the shadow of a brewery in one of the city's blue-collar neighborhoods. At The Seattle Mirror, he is competing for the single full-time job being offered through the paper's intense intern program. But unlike the program's other young reporters, who attended big name schools and worked at other big metro dailies, Wade put himself through community college, and lacked the same experience. Wade struggles with his haunting past as he pursues the story of Karen Harding, a college student whose car was found abandoned on a lonely stretch of highway in the Pacific Northwest. How could this beloved young woman with the altruistic nature simply vanish? Wade battles mounting odds and cut-throat competition to unearth the truth behind Karen Harding's disturbing case. Her disappearance is a story he cannot give up, never realizing the toll it could exact from him. The Dying Hour is a bone-chilling, mesmerizing page-turner that introduces readers to an all-too-human young hero who journeys into the darkest regions of the human heart to confront a nightmare. The International Thriller Writers (ITW), selected The Dying Hour as a finalist for a Thriller Award for Best Paperback Original, 2006.Rick Mofina is a former journalist who has interviewed murderers on death row, flown over L.A. with the LAPD and patrolled with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police near the Arctic. He's also reported from the Caribbean, Africa and Kuwait's border with Iraq. His books have been published in nearly 30 countries, including an illegal translation produced in Iran. His work has been praised by James Patterson, Dean Koontz, Michael Connelly, Lee Child, Tess Gerritsen, Jeffery Deaver, Sandra Brown, James Rollins, Brad Thor, Nick Stone, David Morrell, Allison Brennan, Heather Graham, Linwood Barclay, Peter Robinson, Håkan Nesser and Kay Hooper.The Crime Writers of Canada, The International Thriller Writers and The Private Eye Writers of America have listed his titles among the best in crime fiction. demonstrations.review: This mystery grabs your attention and won't let you go until you finish the book.  Can't wait to read more from this talented author.  Every one of his books I've read has been fantastic and hard to put down without reading it in one marathon session.

target.item_text:
Glyphic (I Am Another Yourself)
Paperback – November 7, 2013

A psychedelic, verse picaresque in the vein of Carlos Castañeda. --Kirkus Review Glyphic is a political novella in verse about an American living in Mexico and Guatemala in the late 1990s when one country was recovering from years and years of civil war and the other had just suffered two massacres of the indigenous Mayan population. The novella is founded in the ooga booga of Latin American magic realism. It examines time, reality, and loyalty as the characters deal with the backlash after peaceful protests. The main characters move through beautiful places and relationships and the narrator finds out who he is and how the world works behind the scenes. The characters experience love, prison, revenge, and Terror. It is a tale of common sense defiance that leads to catharsis and rejuvenation. This leaves the main character with the tough choice to either beat down the powers that be or leave it to others and marry the fiancee. The style is layered and complex.
target.review: I wasn't sure what I would be getting when I first started this, but all too quickly I was swept up in this lyrical novella that manages to be exciting and dramatic while calm and peaceful at the same time. Ralph-Michael Chiaia weaves a story of a journey through life, time and self in a truly beautiful and heartfelt way. What I liked best about this novel was that it had this timeless quality to it that resonated with me, a collected of events and circumstances mixed together with beautiful cultures and the experiences of life that bind us all together. The author has a talent for storytelling that is clear through the story, pulling the reader in and keeping a tight hold on you until you've reached the end and sit back in thought. It's well-paced, beautifully vivid with imagery and has a fantastic plot that never wanes, overall it was well worth the read and it's something I would certainly recommend to other readers.

Book Authority: How to Write, Self-Publish & Market Your Book

No Fluff, Just Stuff! Before you spent hours researching or dollars on your HOW TO questions related book, take a pause to spend an hour or two reading this book. Your time and money will be WORTH spent! I will take you all through my journey of how my first authored book Millionomics got ranked 112TH BEST SELLER BOOK OVERALL on Amazon during special promotion period. Book Authority is a deep dive concise attempt into touching on all KEY aspects of book Writing , Self-Publishing , and Marketing! This book is designed to help authors who are looking to self publish their own books. I truly believe that readers will gain valuable insights from this book as I touch on each and every aspect on the below set of points in the book: • When should one pursue their passion for writing a book • How to pursue writing the book (First step forward) • Various software tools available for self publish • How to overcome some of the most common, and uncommon technical challenges • How to structure your book • How to keep the focus on important aspects of your book • How to get your book edited • How much will it cost you to publish the book • How to get the book designed including getting an effective cover page • Why Cover page and book design is critical to success • Ways you can cost effectively get all of your work freelanced and integrate it all together • How and when to reach out to your network for initial feedback and pursue final editing • How to self publish the “e” book version of your book across various platforms • How to self publish the “print” version of your book across various platforms • Should you go for Audio version of the book, and, if so, how to self publish your Audio book • Deep dive into various self publishing platforms • How to overcome some of the most common and uncommon self publishing challenges • Ways to market your book and ways to make some money (I guess that’s one of our goals too!) • How to approach bloggers and well known book reviewers on top websites • How to build your Social presence and market your cause • What other ways and venues you should gradually consider to expand your reach • Ways to respond to the reviews and questions • How to closely track your success • How to schedule everything • How not to lose heart easily, or, in other words don’t give up! • It’s a never ending process of marketing a self published work
demonstrations.review:
I have to say that when I first went looking for hep in not only honing my writing into an actual book and then publishing it I was a bit overwhelmed by all the books, resources and contradicting information. Then a fellow writer recommended "Book Authority: How to Write, Self-Publish & Market Your Book" and I was immediately set on an informative path to creating and self-publishing my own book. Shiv Verma does a wonderful job of keeping the book down-to-earth and straightforward, keeping the information, advice and tips concise and practical from start to finish.

This is the kind of guide that provides you with a solid foundation for writing your book and then skillfully guides you through the intricate process of publishing it and then getting the word out about it with successful marketing techniques. I learned a great deal from this guide to the point that I made the final leap and have begun the tireless task of getting my idea for a book to paper so I can turn it into a successful (and profitable) eBook. Overall, this was a great choice for me as a new author and as a self-publisher. I would certainly recommend it to other authors looking to make headway in this tumultuous publishing world.

demonstrations.review: "The Last Dragon Slayer" is one of those fantasy novels that starts off with a bang and keeps you eagerly reading until the very end, only to leave you bouncing in your seat waiting for the next novel in the series. demonstrations.item_text:
At Their Own Game (The SpoCompton series Book 1)

But times are tough, so he decides to step up to the big money with a drug deal. Everything that can go wrong, does. demonstrations.review: At Their Own Game is the kind of fast-paced crime novel that hooks you from the very beginning and sends you on a truly action-packed adventure. Frank Zafiro delves into the world of smalltime criminals with bigtime dreams as Jake Stankovic makes the push to take his stolen property racket to the next level with a drug deal... only to find things spiraling way out of control. The well-written and engaging story has all the makings of a fantastic novel, from hair-raising action to emotionally charged drama and everything in between. Overall, it was a very entertaining read that certainly kept me sucked into the story until the very end.

demonstrations.item_text:
Plague of Angels
Kindle Edition

She's the Queen of Hell. He's the Son of God. They'll end humanity… together. Nyx is the ruler of the banished Angels. When her flock returns home, she's stuck on Earth with none other than the Son of God. Surprisingly, God's son tells her he was tricked into sacrificing himself for a cause he doesn't believe in - mankind's redemption. As his mortal body dies, the Son of God offers the Queen of Hell a paradise on Earth if she completes a single mission: helping him obliterate humanity. Nyx launches a thousand-year campaign of violence, sex, and betrayal to force God's people to worship her instead. From the back streets of Jerusalem to the Pope's bedchamber, Nyx and her companions work to destroy the worshippers of God. What Nyx doesn't realize is that her arrangement with God's son isn't as simple as it seems. Pick up Plague of Angels to start the frightening and page-turning series today!
demonstrations.review:
As a debut novel for author John Patrick Kennedy, Plague of Angels is an original and refreshing novel that mixes angels, demons, the Son of God and a war on humanity and heaven alike into a thrilling and exciting story that I couldn't put down. This is the kind of novel that sparks with imagination and creativity, there are no boundaries to keep the story hindered and no stone left unturned to keep the plot from fully achieving its goal of entertaining the reader.

The story revolves around Nyx, the undisputed leader of the Angels who have fallen known as The Descended, and how her fateful meeting with the Son of God that changes the fates of both Earth and Heaven in unimaginable ways. What follows is a campaign of war against humanity as Nyx that is thrilling in its excess and it's non-stop plummet into sex, violence, revenge, betrayal and intrigue.The relationship between Nyx and God's son is complicated and mysterious, but you can't help but be captivated by them as the havoc they wreck continues to unfold.

Overall, this was an exciting novel that certainly kept me sucked into the plot from beginning to end. I am really eager to see what else John Patrick Kennedy comes up with in the future.

demonstrations.item_text:

Paperback – October 1, 2013

Have you ever wanted to get inked, but you were too afraid? Do you already have a tattoo, but are still clueless as to what actually happened while you were in the chair?  Are you a tattoo artist looking for a way to explain everything to those pesky clients who ask a billion questions? C.R. Jordan, author of Basic Fundamentals of Modern Tattoo and creator of TeachMeToTattoo.com takes the mystery out of the tattoo process and the tattoo industry. demonstrations.review:
"This Might Sting a Bit" is an entertaining glimpse into the world of tattoos; it's the kind of book that you didn't you you always wanted to read until you actually read it. It's filled with interesting tidbits about the tattoo process as well as helpful advice that everyone who wants a tattoo needs to know; it roots up facts and figures about tattoos and the procedure used for them... basically taking what would have been a flat, one-dimensional black ink tattoo and giving it depth and color to bring it to life.

C.R. Jordan has a gift for writing that helps to explore and explain tattoos in a fun way, not only entertaining the reader but allowing them to learn a few things as well. From helpful advice about after-care to what to look for when you want to find a tattoo artist, "This Might Sting a Bit" really does tell you everything you need to know about tattoos for before and after you get a tattoo. Overall, it gave me a wealth of information and knowledge about tattoos that I didn't know I needed; I"ll certainly be using the knowledge gained from the book the next time I get a tattoo.

From the New York Times bestselling author of The Diamond Eye comes a riveting short story about an impossible connection across two centuries that could make the difference between peace or war. Yorkshire, 1943. Lily Baines, a bright young debutante increasingly ground down by an endless war, has traded in her white gloves for a set of headphones. It’s her job to intercept enemy naval communications and send them to Bletchley Park for decryption. One night, she picks up a transmission that isn’t code at all—it’s a cry for help. An American ship is taking heavy fire in the North Atlantic—but no one else has reported an attack, and the information relayed by the young US officer, Matt Jackson, seems all wrong. The contact that Lily has made on the other end of the radio channel says it’s…2023. target.review:
What a great book!!! A very interesting and informative book on Apes. The characters are well developed, both chimps and humans. demonstrations.item_text:
Cases, Battles, and Blessings of a Lifetime
Paperback – November 18, 2022

In May 1981, R. Timothy McCrum had just finished his first year of law school. Although, he had no full-time job or tangible prospects, he did have a fiancé who believed in him. In love and filled with optimism, McCrum and his new bride, Andrea, boarded a plane in Pittsburgh and headed to Oregon to create a new life together, never envisioning that twenty-four years later, they would build a beautiful log vacation home on the same Pennsylvania lake where they honeymooned.  In a fascinating retelling of his life story, McCrum details his law career based in the nation’s capital from the Ronald Reagan administration through the Trump era as he practiced both in public service and with a major law firm. He reveals insights into dozens of cases from the unique perspective of a lawyer who battled the federal government and environmental activist groups at all levels of the federal courts. McCrum also describes the blessings of family life and the challenges of balancing his demanding career obligations with that family life, his personal travels, and how his Catholic faith was reawakened later in his career.  Cases, Battles, and Blessings of a Lifetime shares the life story of a seasoned Washington, DC, attorney that highlights his forty years of legal battles, his family life, and his Catholic faith.
demonstrations.review:
Cases, Battles and Blessing is Tim McCrum’s first book and delves into the mining industry and mining law. You don’t realize how ignorant you are of the impact of this large industry on our lives and the economic well-being of our nation. When you pick up the book and see that there are chapter after chapter of “case studies” of mining cases argued in court, you think this is going to be “BORING!!” Actually, the book is quite interesting for Tim covers the cases from a legal standpoint, his role whether major or minor, and the various rulings that are handed down. His humor is interspersed in the descriptions of the cases, and you really get to understand what is at stake in each and every case. Tim is a “hands-on” lawyer in that he visits the mining sites to gain a personal understanding of the issues. Tim didn’t just sit at his desk in Washington D.C. but traveled to many of the western states, to Guatemala, and El Salvador researching the cases. He is involved in the industry foundations and associations and has made many key contacts which he uses as key witnesses for his cases.

Many mining cases take years to be resolved and the lawyers on both sides are working diligently for four or six or more years. Most mining for minerals are on National Forest and public (government own/leased) properties managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). The cases included in this book are all cases of mining companies or mines owned by private individuals on private land challenging the enforcement or interpretation of the mining laws by the Department of the Interior and Department of Justice. With his diligent research into background facts, locale facts, and legal precedent, Tim would argue his cases effectively and win. He who has the most knowledge and can present facts and figures in a clear concise manner will win. Tim is that lawyer! He has been recognized as the top lawyer in mining for over 20 years.

The book includes cases and his perspective up until he retired in 2021. The law firm was definitely affected by the Covid shutdown. As in many businesses virtual meetings became the method of doing business. However, before this Tim could see the writing on the wall where people were scattering, loyalty was lacking in the workplace, trust and congeniality were on the downward slope. Many of his law partners and person friends at the law firm were retiring from 2010-2020 and new people who didn’t have the same political persuasion or personal involvement were now a large part of the firm. The core values were changing with this turnover in personnel.

Interspersed in the 47 chapters are chapters on his and Andrea’s personal lives and challenges. Five children all of whom are well educated, married, and parents to 11 grandchildren are the joy of their lives.

demonstrations.item_text:
Alan Turing: Unlocking the Enigma (Kindle Single)
Kindle Edition

Alan Mathison Turing. Mathematician, philosopher, codebreaker, a founder of computer science, and the father of Artificial Intelligence, Turing was one of the most original thinkers of the last century - and the man whose work helped create the computer-driven world we now inhabit.  But he was also an enigmatic figure, deeply reticent yet also strikingly naïve. Turing’s openness about his homosexuality at a time when it was an imprisonable offense ultimately led to his untimely death at the age of only forty-one. In 'Alan Turing: Unlocking the Enigma', David Boyle reveals the mysteries behind the man and his remarkable career. Aged just 22, Turing was elected a fellow at King's College, Cambridge on the strength of a dissertation in which he proved the central limit theorem. By the age of 33, he had been awarded the OBE by King George VI for his wartime services: Turing was instrumental in cracking the Nazi Enigma machines at the top secret code breaking establishment at Bletchley Park during the Second World War. But his achievements were to be tragically overshadowed by the paranoia of the post-War years. Hounded for his supposedly subversive views and for his sexuality, Turing was prosecuted in 1952, and forced to accept the humiliation of hormone treatment to avoid a prison sentence. Just two years later, at the age of 41 he was dead. The verdict: cyanide poisoning. Was Turing’s death accidental as his mother always claimed? Or did persistent persecution drive him to take him own life? ‘Alan Turing: Unlocking the Enigma’ seeks to find the man behind the science, illuminating the life of a person who is still a shadowy presence behind his brilliant achievements. David Boyle's work has been widely praised. David Boyle is a British author and journalist who writes mainly about history and new ideas in economics, money, business and culture. He lives in Crystal Palace, London. His books include ‘Unheard Unseen: Warfare in the Dardanelles’, ‘Towards the Setting Sun: The Race for America’ and ‘The Age to Come’. Endeavour Press is the UK's leading independent publisher of digital books.

“Elvis Cole provides more fun for the reader than any L.A. private eye to come along in years.”—Joseph Wambaugh WINNER OF THE ANTHONY AND MACAVITY AWARDS FOR BEST NOVEL • NOMINATED FOR THE EDGAR AND SHAMUS AWARDS FOR BEST NOVEL Meet Elvis Cole, L.A. target.review:
Finally, a mystery/thriller series I love. This book was outstanding. Having read all of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher series, I’ve been fighting withdrawal by hunting a new series to replace it. The Elvis Cole series exceeded my expectations.

First, Robert Crais’ writing style is right up my alley. He’s hard boiled but has a well developed character in Elvis Cole. Elvis is hilarious, quick witted, and 180 degrees different than other detectives. He’s caring and sensitive when appropriate. He’s obsessed with Disney. Cole has Disney decor all throughout his office. This is a great spin on a hard boiled protagonist.

I’ll continue to read through this entire series for sure. My only dislike is the same dislike I have with all adult fiction-the language and adult content. This was occasional, but take this as a warning. Robert Crais is a master mystery writer and I’m impressed.

demonstrations.item_text:
Mr. Mercedes: A Novel (1) (The Bill Hodges Trilogy)
Paperback – January 6, 2015

Now an AT&T Audience Original Series WINNER OF THE EDGAR AWARD FOR BEST NOVEL #1 New York Times bestseller! In a high-suspense race against time, three of the most unlikely heroes Stephen King has ever created try to stop a lone killer from blowing up thousands. “ Mr. Mercedes is a rich, resonant, exceptionally readable accomplishment by a man who can write in whatever genre he chooses” ( The Washington Post ). In the frigid pre-dawn hours, in a distressed Midwestern city, desperate unemployed folks are lined up for a spot at a job fair. Without warning, a lone driver plows through the crowd in a stolen Mercedes, running over the innocent, backing up, and charging again. Eight people are killed; fifteen are wounded. The killer escapes.  In another part of town, months later, a retired cop named Bill Hodges is still haunted by the unsolved crime. When he gets a crazed letter from someone who self-identifies as the “perk” and threatens an even more diabolical attack, Hodges wakes up from his depressed and vacant retirement, hell-bent on preventing another tragedy.  Brady Hartsfield lives with his alcoholic mother in the house where he was born. He loved the feel of death under the wheels of the Mercedes, and he wants that rush again. Only Bill Hodges, with two new, unusual allies, can apprehend the killer before he strikes again. And they have no time to lose, because Brady’s next mission, if it succeeds, will kill or maim thousands. Mr. Mercedes is a war between good and evil, from the master of suspense whose insight into the mind of this obsessed, insane killer is chilling and unforgettable.
demonstrations.review:
I could’ve missed work to stay up reading this adrenaline rush.

My review is filtered through the mind of a first time King reader. I’m a Lee Child fanatic who’s branched out in several different directions. I’ve always respected Stephen King. I’ve listened to him speak on Youtube and read scores of articles about him.

I read Mr. Mercedes first because it’s a thriller in the mystery/detective category which I’m most fond of. I instantly understand where all his praise comes from. King’s not just writing books, he’s writing literature. No one will guess that this is his first detective work. I can’t wait for Finder Keeper’s to come out staring the same three protagonist.

Only down side for me was the increased language in this novel. Also, King went above and beyond in the fleshing out of the villain, and did an excellent job at it. Although, this is where things get weird, but true to life. The antagonist is a surrogate husband. This part is disgusting. This is a common thread for psychopaths, so I don’t blame King for adding it in. But I never would’ve taken to detail the way he did.

demonstrations.review:
Awards: Anthony Award and Barry Award for best first novel

Let's be honest. Killing Floor, Lee Child's debut novel, has been summarized a few times. Agree? Nevertheless, we scourer the net in search of a couple answers-should I read the suddenly popular Jack Reacher series? Must I stick to them in original order? Considering you know the plot, and can download the sample chapter on Amazon, here's my thoughts.

Killing Floor blew me away from the beginning. I hate to waste time with a dire novel. If I'm reading a series you can bet it's worth it. In a sentence, Jack Reacher is an astonishing protagonist, other characters are fleshed out, and the rangy plot adds depth and adventure. Midway through the characters leap off the page. I was sad when it ended. Left me feeling like I was moving away from my neighborhood friends.

I read reviews criticizing Child's prose and choppy sentences-stating he's no Hemingway. In defense, this writer birthed one of the most prodigious characters in action/suspense history. Truth be told, anyone who endeavors Hemingway's long winding style will fall short. Child strike's me as a master writer, and this book had me ordering the second three quarters of the way through.

I hope that tackled both questions. In my opinion if your interested in the series, then start with book one and read them in order. Why would you not? It's just as simple as that folks.

Last thought, upon finishing Killing Floor, I watched interviews of Child, and made a connection to the series' popularity. Jack Reacher completes a void in the hearts of modern society. He's an alienated vagabond living a minimalist life. He tries to avoid trouble, but for the sake of the readers, manages to walk into a mess. How he gets out has developed a cult following. He puts the order in law and order, and he does it with a six-five frame of force. He could care less about the law when justice is at stake. He's the strong silent type with infinite competence. A nobleman and something we've missed for a long time.

#1 BESTSELLER • Ben Mears has returned to Jerusalem’s Lot in hopes that exploring the history of the Marsten House, an old mansion long the subject of rumor and speculation, will help him cast out his personal devils and provide inspiration for his new book. But when two young boys venture into the woods, and only one returns alive, Mears begins to realize that something sinister is at work.In fact, his hometown is under siege from forces of darkness far beyond his imagination. And only he, with a small group of allies, can hope to contain the evil that is growing within the borders of this small New England town.With this, his second novel, Stephen King established himself as an indisputable master of American horror, able to transform the old conceits of the genre into something fresh and all the more frightening for taking place in a familiar, idyllic locale.
demonstrations.review:
I don’t want to say that this is one of the greatest works of fiction I’ve ever read, but that’s exactly what I’m saying. I’m new to Stephen King. I’ve only read Mr. Mercedes as my introduction into his works. It led me to go back and read the works he’s known for. Now, I fully understand how these are classics. Not only in horror fiction, but in general.

My mind is tangled up trying to put a finger on how King does it. I just put down this book and I’m amazed at how well the prose flowed. It read itself. The story was astonishing, if there’s even a word to describe it. Needless to mention, I give the prose 5 stars.

I loved the characters. Even the unlikable ones, if that makes sense. King has a way with characters that I haven’t come across before. I truly cared for them. They were real. No one else that I’ve read rivals his characters, storytelling, and beautiful, but understated language.

The premise of this book was right up King’s alley, as I know he writes a lot about small towns. Salem’s Lot is a small town plot that he paints beautifully with outstanding imagery. This book was thrilling, in a familiar way and indifferent. Chapters were devoted to nothing but town imagery, the locals and their routine, although, somehow, it was compelling to read every word. These chapters weren’t boring, not at the least. They were great. The rest was chill bump rising fun, adrenaline soaked scenes, and white knuckle anticipation.

Do I recommend this book? If you haven’t read Stephen King’s classics, go back in time like I did and devour these timeless works of art.

The New York Times bestseller featured on 60 Minutes , this is the first book to take readers inside the world of elite Navy SEAL dogs. As Seen on "60 Minutes"! As a Navy SEAL during a combat deployment in Iraq, Mike Ritland saw a military working dog in action and instantly knew he'd found his true calling. Ritland started his own company training and supplying dogs for the SEAL teams, U.S. Government, and Department of Defense. He knew that fewer than 1 percent of all working dogs had what it takes to contribute to the success of our nation's elite combat units, and began searching the globe for animals who fit this specific profile. These specialized canines had to pass rigorous selection tests before their serious training could begin.The results were a revelation: highly trained working dogs capable of handling both detection and apprehension work in the most extreme environments and the tensest of battlefield conditions. Though fiercely aggressive and athletic, these dogs develop a close bond with the handlers they work side by side with and the other team members. Truly integrating themselves into their units, these K9 warriors are much like their human counterparts—unwavering in their devotion to duty, strong enough and tough enough to take it to the enemy through pain, injury, or fear.For the first time ever, the New York Times bestseller Trident K9 Warriors gives readers an inside look at these elite canines—who they are, how they are trained, and the extreme missions they undertake saving countless lives, asking for little in the way of reward. From detecting explosives to eliminating the bad guys, these powerful dogs are also some of the smartest and most highly skilled working animals on the planet.
target.review: I am a disabled civilian who once had the incredible honor of working with a police department's K-9 unit for a year or so. It was one of the best times of my life. So very many thanks for a great book, but many million more for what you have and are doing for my beloved country and the animals and people that protect her freedoms. God bless you.

The book then flashes back to the events of Christmas Eve, 1988, during which Walt Longmire convinced Lucian Connolly to fly a battered WWII vintage B-25 to Denver in a blizzard to try to save the life of a little girl severely burned in a car crash in Montana. It's not so much a mystery as a harrowing recounting of these men doing the right thing regardless of danger to themselves. The book is only 146 pages, and I read it during a long soak in the bathtub. Fans of the Longmire TV series will enjoy this, as will anyone who likes a good story. My only disappointment was that this is a paperback book, and doesn't feel all that high quality; I love purchasing hard covered books, which will last a much longer time.

target.item_text:
Thirteen Reasons Why
Paperback – June 14, 2011

THE #1 NEW YORK TIMES AND INTERNATIONAL BESTSELLER **THE BOOK THAT STARTED IT ALL, NOW A NETFLIX ORIGINAL SERIES** “Eerie, beautiful, and devastating.” — Chicago Tribune “A stealthy hit with staying power. . . . thriller-like pacing.” — The New York Times “ Thirteen Reasons Why will leave you with chills long after you have finished reading.” — Amber Gibson, NPR’s “All Things Considered” You can’t stop the future. You can’t rewind the past. The only way to learn the secret . . . is to press play. Clay Jensen returns home from school to find a strange package with his name on it lying on his porch. Inside he discovers several cassette tapes recorded by Hannah Baker—his classmate and crush—who committed suicide two weeks earlier. Hannah's voice tells him that there are thirteen reasons why she decided to end her life. Clay is one of them. If he listens, he'll find out why.                   Clay spends the night crisscrossing his town with Hannah as his guide. He becomes a firsthand witness to Hannah's pain, and as he follows Hannah’s recorded words throughout his town, what he discovers changes his life forever. Need to talk? Call 1-800-273-TALK (8255) anytime if you are in the United States. It’s free and confidential. Find more resources at 13reasonswhy.info. Find out how you can help someone in crisis at bethe1to.com.
target.review:
This character, Hannah, was obviously mentally ill. I cannot imagine anyone committing suicide for the reasons that she did (unless the character were much younger). I don't think that any of her reasons were why - - She killed herself because she was full of anger and needed to take revenge on anyone who hurt her in the slightest.

This book needed to make two points very clear, which it never did :

(1) If you kill yourself, no matter why, it is your choice and you are to blame.
If any other person was truly to blame for your suicide, then that other person would go to jail for murder.

(2) There are so many ways to deal with problems, and suicide is a permanent act that solves nothing - - if revenge is the goal, there are other ways to get revenge other than ending your life. If your death did succeed in getting revenge, at some point, those people will move on, because you can't expect them to feel guilt forever. But your life will be over forever.

This book needed to send an important message, which it never did :

* * * No matter how depressed you are, and no matter how bad you believe your life is, there is always hope. If you get help, you don't know how tomorrow can bring changes.

Hannah did not want help. There were so many characters in this book who cared about her. The proof of this is that her tapes were listened to. For example, if Clay did not care about Hannah, then he would not have listened to the tapes - - he would have simply thrown them away. Hannah had to know that people cared about her, because she believed that people would take the time to listen to her very long tapes. If Hannah found school so unbearable, then she could have asked to change schools or be home-schooled, or she could have dropped out.

It is a good thing that this is a novel and not a true story. Hannah was young, beautiful, heathy, strong, and she had her whole life ahead of her, with years of possibilities that were wasted. It takes a strong and determined and intelligent and creative person to make those kinds of tapes and distribute them - - she could have used all of that energy to seek help.

What bothers me most about the topic of suicide is what a waste it is. Life is so short. Life is so precious. There are so many sick people who are fighting for their lives while there are so many healthy people who are throwing their lives away.

It is scary that a very young person, or a mentally ill person, may read this book and use it as a manual.

demonstrations.item_text:
For Love of Audrey Rose
Kindle Edition

The sequel to Audrey Rose takes Janice Templeton back to the death of Audrey Rose and the mystery of where she is if she was reincarnated as Ivy Templeton. Ivy, Janice's daughter, was also killed in a car crash. Janice is determined to find the truth.
demonstrations.review:
I read the original book, "Audrey Rose," and I totally loved it.

Later, I saw the movie, with Marsha Mason and John Beck and Susan Swift.
The movie was just okay.
It did not have the thrills that the book had.

So, I wanted to read this sequel, and it was really disappointing.
Mostly, I was shocked that this sequel was written by the same author who wrote the first book (because this second book was written with many incorrect statements from the first book).

This book starts out with a prologue, which is many pages of basically a summary of the first book (either to remind the reader of the first book, or to fill the reader in if you haven't read the first book) - - but this summary is full of things that never happened in the first book, and things that are just incorrect.

This book was way too long - - this sequel could have been half the size - - it felt like reading two sequels in one book.

This book was very sad and depressing, all the way through - - it was just constant misery.
This book is about reincarnation, but it mostly felt like it was about grieving parents who could not let go of a deceased child.

Many times in this book, a character would say something positive, but immediately followed by something negative.
For example, "We all loved Ivy and we know that her death was inevitable and that her soul has been set free.... but Ivy's soul cannot rest because she died so horribly, so her soul must be in constant torment, and every new life that she has will be doomed."

There was no action in this book.
It just dragged on, just getting more and more depressing.

demonstrations.item_text:
Forever . . .
Paperback – April 29, 2014

A Time Best YA Book of All Time (2021) Judy Blume’s groundbreaking novel about first relationships, first love, and…the first time . The bed is brass, covered with a patchwork quilt, and “nice and firm,” Michael says, “in case you’re interested.” Katherine is interested. Katherine and Michael are in love, and Katherine knows it’s forever—especially after she loses her virginity to him. But when they’re separated for the summer, she begins to have feelings for another boy. What does this say about her love for Michael? And what does “forever” mean, anyway? Is this the love of a lifetime, or the very beginning of a lifetime of love?
demonstrations.review:
CONTAINS SPOILERS .......

Judy Blume is used to writing children's books for small children.
She doesn't know how to write for anyone older, which is why all of her sentences are so simple.
She is afraid to use a word stronger than first grade level vocabulary because she believes that her reader will not understand.

"Forever" is, therefore, a very simple book.
Katherine and Michael meet, just like "Run, Spot, Run!"
There is a female teenager and a male teenager - - no reason to go into any more detail - - that is all that is necessary for Judy Blume's readers.

Katherine and Michael barely know each other's names, and it is time for sex.
They have nothing in common - - Michael rides horses and likes to ski, and Katherine dances and plays tennis.
Katherine says "no" a few times, and then just lays right down on the colorful carpet and gives it all away.
I would have appreciated some romance, some conversation, some detail, some description about where Katherine was, what was happening, what she was feeling physically and emotionally, and why - - this book left me with so many Whys.

The only part of this book that meant anything to me was the article that Katherine forced herself to read.
That line: "Have you thought about how this relationship will end?" stayed with me.
That line is good advice to everyone in any new relationship, even if it isn't a romantic relationship.

What is missing from this book?
Katherine never describes what Forever feels like.
For example . . .

Does she feel like she is floating on a cloud - - like life is suddenly so much more beautiful?
Does she feel like she wants to shout it from the rooftops to anyone who will listen, how amazing love feels?
Does she feel compelled to write love letters to Michael, or even to write poetry?

Katherine never describes how she feels about Michael, or how she feels when they are together.
Is he her best friend, her soul mate, the love of her life?
Is he absolutely everything to her, does she feel like she cannot live without him?
Does she feel like every love song that she has ever heard is all about him?
What does it feel like to hold his hand - - is there electricity?
Does she feel a pull toward him, like a magnet?
Does she ever sneak glances at him when he doesn't know, peek at the bulge in his jeans with curiosity, look up and down at his naked body and crave touching him everywhere?

Does she feel like he is her other half, like she is complete when she is with him?
How does it feel to look into his eyes - - does she get lost in them, like two become one?
Does it feel like they don't need words, but also that they want to tell each other every little thing?
How does it feel when he holds her - - how does it feel when he kisses her - - how does it feel when he says her name in the dark?

Does she imagine, in detail, him proposing to her?
Does she scribble in her notebook - - Katherine Wagner, Mrs. Michael Wagner, Mr. and Mrs. Wagner, etc.?
Does she look through bridal magazines and choose wedding gowns that she might like to wear?
Does she stop at jewelry store windows and look at the engagement rings?
Or does she imagine running away with him to elope and then having a secret honeymoon?
Does she imagine having a child with him - - creating a perfect little person who shares both of their features - - would they name him Michael Junior?
Does she wonder how many children they would have and what their names could be, what pets they might have and what they might name them, what kind of a house they would live in, and where they would go on family vacations?

They used the word "Forever," but while lying in bed naked together, did they ever talk about their future together and make plans?

This is what "Forever" is supposed to be about.
A reader who has never been in love would want to hear about this.
A reader who has been in love and who has had a broken heart would want something to relate to.

I don't think that Judy Blume has ever been passionately in love.
I don't think that Judy Blume has ever had a broken heart.
If she has, then she simply is not a good writer, because none of the feelings that I could write, as I wrote above, were in this book.

I hated the character of Michael.
I saw Michael as a teenage boy who only wanted sex - - the kind of sex that is quick where he doesn't care about his partner's feelings.
I hated the way that Michael pressured her to have sex, with little coaxing remarks such as, "Like always, Kath."

I saw Katherine as an average teenage girl, but lacking self-worth so that Michael could manipulate her.
Katherine, like many teenage girls, thought that she was in love just as soon as some guy showed her a little attention.

I think that Michael was about to dump her if he didn't get sex soon.
I think that it was all about "love" for Katherine, but it was all about "sex" for Michael.
I was surprised that Michael bothered to take Katherine away on a skiing trip, until I realized that it was his big plan to get her alone for sex - - other than that trip, what did they do together as a couple, except have sex?

What would Michael have done if Katherine had gotten pregnant?
I can imagine him doing a few different hurtful things, but mostly, leaving her as quickly as possible.
Maybe I am too hard on the character of Michael - - or maybe Judy Blume didn't write him so that the reader could know him - - but I didn't feel any love coming from him.
The only thing that Michael did that I appreciated was to give Katherine a necklace.

I understand that Katherine is the narrator, so we only get her perspective on everything, but a good writer would have found a way to let the reader in on Michael's feelings and motives - - such as something simple, like Katherine overhearing a conversation between Michael and anyone else.

I would have appreciated some deep conversations between Katherine and Erica - - Erica was Katherine's best friend, but they never talked.

Michael's rude comment, in front of everyone, "I have a headache that is not to be believed,"
followed by Katherine's simple, pathetic response, "Take two aspirin," summed up their relationship for me - -
In other words, have sex and everything is fine . . . don't have sex, and we have a problem.

Michael actually gave his "thing" a name - - he named it Ralph.
Does anyone know that the word Ralph is sometimes slang for throwing up?
I found this disgusting and not at all romantic.
He could have named it something classy like Reginald or Rupert or Randolph - - or even Richard because we all know one of the nicknames for Richard.
I think that Judy Blume found it necessary to give it a name because she felt uncomfortable, as a writer, using the word for that body part.
But Katherine's body part doesn't deserve a name?

I didn't like the ending.
Michael and Katherine are apart for the summer, and as soon as they see each other again, Michael can't wait to get her back into bed.
She won't, as usual, just lay down for him, and he immediately blames it on her grandfather's death.
He can't imagine that there could be any other reason for her not giving it all up to him.
And I didn't see any sympathies coming from Michael toward Katherine when her grandfather died - - did he even bother to send flowers or even a card?
After a long time apart, Katherine won't just jump into bed, so Michael breaks up with her.
The back cover of my version of the book says, "The first time, a loving time, but what about Forever?"

I hated when Michael cruelly confessed that he cheated on her while they were apart for the summer - - the way that he said, "You might as well know, I screwed my way around."
Katherine is so stupid that she doesn't believe him, and she says, "You are just saying that to hurt me."
He says, "You will never know, though, will you?" and he just drives away, and she just stands there, wondering if he really cheated on her.
Of course he cheated on her while they were apart . . . and he probably also cheated on her while they were together, the entire time.

Katherine wondered how she could have feelings for Theo if she loved Michael so much.
Easy answer - - She didn't really love Michael.
She just had romantic ideas in her head and gave them all to Michael (again, ideas which we never actually hear about) - - She wanted to be in love, so she was in love with love, not the person.

What did I expect at the end of the book?
Here is how I would have ended the book . . .

I expected Katherine to be home, thinking about the end of Forever, maybe holding her necklace in her hand.
She would maybe throw the necklace, and throw everything that she can get her hands on.
Then cry, scream, sob, punch pillows.

It would be normal to run to her mother and tell her that she can't believe that it is over and that she can't stand it.
And her mother would hug her and say something like, "Michael will probably call... It isn't likely that it is all over just like that."

And then Katherine would run to Erica, and Erica would say that Michael is a creep, and say something like,
"So, why don't you fight for your love? If you love him, then go to him and tell him that you want to work things out."

That doesn't happen.
Michael never calls again.
Katherine never calls him again.
They both just give up.
And what exactly did they break up over? Sex? So, they got together based on sex and they broke up for the same reason.

Katherine doesn't describe her feelings about the end of Forever,
such as as hurt, pain, anger, betrayal, feeling used, feeling like a fool, confusion, loneliness, etc.
She doesn't discuss her feelings with anyone, such as her mother, friend, or sister.
She doesn't even need to get it out by writing it down in a diary or in a letter or in a poem, or by ripping up his picture and throwing it into the fireplace.
Instead, the reader gets a flat comment from her mother that, "Theo called." And we know that Katherine is going to rush to return that call.

What does the reader get from the end of this book?
Forever is over very quickly and easily.
It isn't worth it to attempt to try to fix Forever.
There is no mourning for the guy, or for the relationship, or for the loss of everything that might have happened in the years of Forever.
Forever simply gets transferred over from Michael to Theo, and even on to the next guy after Theo.
So, Judy Blume's definition of Forever is not "For Ever," but "For Months."

Too many other reviewers give Judy Blume's writing a break, blaming it on the characters' ages.
I find that very insulting - - Do you all really believe that two high school seniors are not capable of the same deep and real love as a couple just a few years older?
There are couples who are "high school sweethearts" and stay together into old age.
And, there are adults who can't hold any relationships together.
I really don't believe that age is an excuse - - I believe that Forever is possible for everyone, whether you are a teen or a lot older.

I think that the characters in this book never had real love and never had a relationship that was based on anything substantial . . . because Judy Blume is not capable of writing about the real "Forever" - - like what I wrote about above.

There is a line from a sitcom theme song :
"It was like I started breathing on the night we kissed, and I can't remember what I ever did before."
Whoever wrote that line knew what "Forever" means.

demonstrations.item_text:
Patience & Sarah (Little Sister's Classics)
Paperback – Illustrated, September 1, 2005

“A remarkable story.”— Publishers Weekly Set in the nineteenth century, Isabel Miller’s classic lesbian novel traces the relationship between Patience White, an educated painter, and Sarah Dowling, a cross-dressing farmer, whose romantic bond does not sit well with the puritanical New England farming community in which they live. They choose to live together and love each other freely, even though they know of no precedents for their relationship; they must trust their own instincts and see beyond the disdain of their neighbors. Ultimately, they are forced to make life-changing decisions that depend on their courage and their commitment to one another. First self-published in 1969 in an edition of one thousand copies, the author hand-sold the book on New York street corners; it garnered increasing attention to the point of receiving the American Library Association’s first Gay Book Award in 1971. McGraw-Hill’s version of the book a year later brought it to mainstream bookstores across the country. Patience & Sarah is a historical romance whose drama was a touchstone for the burgeoning gay and women’s activism of the late 1960s and early 1970s. It celebrates the joys of an uninhibited love between two strong women with a confident defiance that remains relevant today. This edition features an appendix of supplementary materials about Patience & Sarah and the author, as well as an introduction by Emma Donoghue, the Irish novelist whose numerous books include the contemporary Dublin novels Stirfry and Hood , the latter of which won the ALA’s Gay and Lesbian Book Award in 1995. Little Sister’s Classics is an Arsenal Pulp Press imprint dedicated to reviving lost and out-of-print gay and lesbian classic books, both fiction and nonfiction. The series is produced in conjunction with Little Sister’s Books, the heroic gay Vancouver bookstore well-known for its anti-censorship efforts. Isabel Miller was the author of numerous novels, including two under her real name, Alma Routsong. She died in 1996.
demonstrations.review:
This book is a sugary sweet romance between two women in the 1800s.

I recommend this for young women who enjoy old fashioned stories.

This is like reading the Little House on the Prairie books, except the characters are lesbians.

demonstrations.item_text:
True North: The Shocking Truth about Yours, Mine and Ours

Tom North is one of the eight North children, who together with the ten Beardsley children, became the family that was featured in the 1968 film, Yours, Mine and Ours, starring Lucille Ball and Henry Fonda, and again in the 2005 version starring Rene Russo and Dennis Quaid. The book begins in the 1950s on Whidbey Island, Washington, where Tom's mother, Helen North, became a widow when she was just thirty years old and pregnant with her eighth child. Not long after, Helen North met and married Frank Beardsley, a man with ten children and the North children were adopted and their names changed to Beardsley. But it wasn't one big happy family, as the movie depicted. When Tom finally left home, he traveled on a journey of survival, self-discovery, and healing. Years later, miraculously led his family in counseling sessions where shocking truths were revealed, he came full circle as he reclaimed his father's name and was finally, True North.
demonstrations.review:
I loved the old movie "Yours Mine and Ours" and I believed that the movie was all true. When I heard about this book, that one of the children wanted to tell the "real" story, that the movie made it look like it was a happy family when the truth was that it was a nightmarish and hellish home, I really wanted to read the book to hear what really happened.

The first few chapters were mildly interesting, basically telling what we already knew, except for a few sentences that he claimed that Lucille Ball said against the father. The rest of the book was boring and slow and unreadable, mostly about him playing sports outside, about his drug use, and a few comments about abuse which did not get into any kind of real detail and were not supported by any of the other children.

I think that this book is all a complete lie or at least an exaggeration of anything that might be true. It is horrible that this book was written after both parents are dead and cannot defend themselves and that none of the other children support this book as true. I think that this author is recovering from drug addiction and has a lot of anger regarding that, and that he saw an opportunity to talk about drug addiction and recovery and use his family's fame and name as an excuse to make his story interesting, which it is not.

I absolutely do not recommend this book. Most of all, it is very boring and dragged out and poorly written, whether you believe the story or not.

demonstrations.item_text:
Behind the Smile: My Journey Out of Postpartum Depression
Hardcover – May 1, 2001

More than one out of 10 new mothers experience post-partum depression (PPD), yet few women seek help. After Marie Osmond, beloved singer and TV talk show host, gave birth to her seventh child (four of her children are adopted), she became increasingly depressed. One night, she handed over her bank card to her babysitter, got in her car, and drove north-with no intention of returning until she had emerged from her crisis. After she went public with her own experiences with PPD on Oprah and Larry King Live , the response was overwhelming. Now collaborating with a doctor who helped her through her ordeal, Marie Osmond will share the fear and depression she overcame, and reveal how she put it all behind her and is moving on with her life.
demonstrations.review:
This book angered me. I didn't believe a word of it.

Marie Osmond was only pregnant twice. All of her other children are adopted.

Marie Osmond had all kinds of help available to her. With her money, she had everything. She had nannies, housekeepers, assistants - - and a large family - - she had so much help available to her - - I am sure that all of these people, together with her doctors, made sure that she was "fine" as she called it.

Marie Osmond has many books out there, such as about her family and career and dolls and sewing, etc. - - so she found another topic for another book. She is constantly on the shopping channels, selling her dolls and endorsing weight loss products. Maybe if she stayed home with her newborn for a little while, then she wouldn't have to whine about how overwhelmed she is. When she wrote about changing the baby's diaper, I didn't even believe that - - where was the nanny? I would have believed that her ten year old daughter changed the diapers more than I believed that Marie Osmond risked ruining her manicure.

Her stories about her childhood were also unbelievable. Sexual abuse? At the age of 3, she buried her mother's jewelry in the backyard? She put peanut butter in her mother's shoes? She talks about how she always had a smile painted on and it was never real - - so why should I believe that anything about her is real, including everything in this book?

If you have ever seen her singing, or on her talk show, or on QVC, then you have seen a confident, well-adjusted, put-together woman - - whether her smile is genuine or not, she certainly is not depressed - - and if she ever was depressed, I am sure that all of those people surrounding her got her the best treatment immediately.

This book is an insult to women who really are suffering. Parts of this book sound like Marie Osmond copied it from a medical journal. Shame on her. This book is as real as her "paper roses."
